articles.title: Trump touts ‘golden age’ at Ohio rally, urges voters to deliver GOP midterm wins
articles.summary: President Donald Trump urged Ohio rally-goers to "pretend I'm on the ballot" as he stumped for Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy in the midterms.
articles.body: President Donald Trump swept into Ohio Saturday night promoting what he calls a new "golden age" for America, pointing to billions of dollars in investment and new jobs in the Buckeye State as he urged voters to help keep Republicans in power in November. For the third time in as many nights, Trump rallied supporters outside Dayton for Republicans Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, casting the midterms as a chance to extend the economic and political gains he said the GOP has delivered since his return to the White House. And with his own name absent from the ballot, Trump gave voters gathered a simple instruction. TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG "Just pretend that I’m running," Trump said. "When I run, we win." Trump, who carried Ohio in all three of his presidential campaigns, later echoed the same message as he sought to rally his political coalition behind Republicans fighting to maintain control of Congress. "If you don’t mind, please pretend that I’m on the ballot," Trump said. "And you need to turn out for a midterm victory." The president used much of the rally to make an economic case for the Republican ticket, declaring Ohio is "booming" as he hailed investments he credited to both his trade and tariff policies. Trump pointed to a $400 million Stellantis investment in Toledo and an $850 million Electra aerospace investment near Springfield. Weaving in an anecdote about his daily aspirin habit, the president also featured Bayer’s plans for a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing campus near Columbus, which the company says will support approximately 600 permanent jobs and 1,500 construction jobs. "Your state is booming," Trump told the gathered crowd. "Every state is booming." FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY Trump credited the investments to his tariff agenda, arguing the U.S. is finally leveling the playing field after years of other countries using tariffs against American products while giving companies a powerful incentive to build at home. The president also threw his support behind Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation aimed at shielding consumers from additional electricity costs associated with data centers. "We want them," Trump said of data centers. "There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China." Husted brought the legislation to the Senate floor days before the rally, where it failed to advance. President Trump pledged to sign it if Congress can send it to his desk. TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE' "I will sign this Ratepayer Protection Act into law immediately," Trump said. Trump broadened his victory lap from Ohio to the country as a whole, hailing stock market records, manufacturing growth, investment and employment while contrasting his own administration’s economic record with former President Joe Biden's. "Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump said. He also praised GOP-backed tax provisions, including no tax on tips and overtime, and reiterated his previously announced proposal for $5,000 payments to adult Americans if Republicans retain the House and Senate. Trump then shifted to immigration and Springfield, Ohio, dedicating his recitation of the poem "The Snake" to the city that became a national flashpoint during the 2024 presidential campaign over an influx of Haitian nationals into the community. "I dedicate this to Springfield, Ohio," Trump said. "They went through hell." After finishing the poem, which the president has long admired as an immigration allegory, he told the crowd, "That’s what happened at our border," before hailing his administration’s immigration crackdown. The president also briefly touched on Venezuela, claiming the U.S. had more than recouped the costs of its military operation against former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro through the country's vast oil resources. "We paid for the cost of the war many, many times over," Trump said. "We’re making a fortune with it." Trump repeatedly weaved the election 31 days away into his remarks, urging Ohioans to support Husted, Ramaswamy and Republican congressional candidates. "If we win the midterms, Ohio will be very, very strongly considered for this," Trump said. "I really want you to go out and vote again for John Husted and for Vivek."

articles.title: Trump, campaigning in Ohio, says the midterms will bring a ‘big surprise’
articles.summary: VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate.
articles.body: VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate. “I think we’re going to have a big surprise, because they don’t know what’s happening,” Trump said while speaking onstage inside a high school gymnasium near Dayton. “Just get out and vote,” Trump added. “If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass.” The visit, part of what White House officials have told NBC News will be a push through at least 17 states between now and Nov. 3, was aimed at boosting incumbent Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP nominee for governor. Trump, who won Ohio three times by comfortable margins, opened his speech with praise for both before moving into broader remarks to promote himself and his administration. He also offered support for local Rep. Mike Turner and for several House candidates in attendance, including Derek Merrin, the Republican running against longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in northwest Ohio. Husted’s bid to keep the Senate seat — which he was appointed to after JD Vance was elected vice president — has in particular become a subject of concern among Republicans in Ohio and Washington. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that Husted’s past enthusiasm for building data centers was hurting his campaign. Others have expressed worries that Husted, who has long wanted to be governor, has not put his full heart into the race. The battle is one of the most expensive and competitive Senate races in the country this fall. Along with a handful of other key contests, the clash between Husted and Brown could determine partisan control of the chamber. This week, Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, poured another $14 million into Ohio to prop up Husted, bringing the group’s investment in the state to $93 million. “Senator Jon Husted votes to put Ohio first, and he votes all the time,” Trump said before relating conversations he’s had with Thune and others: “They think he’s phenomenal.” The high school gym where Trump spoke Saturday night was a smaller venue than has been typical for his rallies. The home court of the Butler High School Aviators seats up to 5,000. There were several stretches of empty seats in upper bleachers as Trump took the stage — and many more by the time he finished speaking 93 minutes later. In Ohio and elsewhere, Republicans are wrestling with how to win at a time when polls show Trump and the war in Iran are highly unpopular and when voters most loyal to Trump might stay home because he’s not on the ballot. “As a lifelong Republican who’s voted in every election since I was 18 and in every primary election as a Republican, I have real concerns that we’re going to be able to turn out the every-four-year Trump voter,” Nick Owens, a former GOP chair in Ohio’s Brown County and former member of the state Board of Education, told NBC News last month. “I have real concerns that those voters just will not come to the polls.” Trump acknowledged that dynamic explicitly Saturday and repeated an argument he’s been making on the campaign trail this fall. “When I run, we win,” Trump said. “But for some reason, when I don’t run, they draw 44% less people. So what I’m going to do is ask you to just pretend that I’m running, because if we do, and if you draw the people, you’re going to win, and we’re going to win big.” Husted, speaking to reporters before the rally, described Trump as a unique asset in his race. “Well, he won Ohio by 11 points in the last election, and if we get those same voters to turn out in this election, we’ll win,” Husted said. Alex Triantafilou, the Ohio GOP chair, told NBC News that the rally was “hugely important” in the effort to motivate those low-propensity, Trump-loyal voters. “We know in Ohio that if we turn out the same electorate that we turned out in 2024, that we’ll win every race,” Triantafilou said in an interview. “Nobody speaks to that crowd better than President Trump.” The Saturday rally included a cameo from Jon Gruden, the former NFL coach who years ago was a teammate of Husted’s on the University of Dayton football team. “Jon Husted is a lot more than my friend,” an animated Gruden told the audience. “He was a great player. … He will never quit on you or anybody.” Trump marveled about Husted’s football-playing days, of which he said he was unaware until hearing about them from Gruden. “Nobody told me you were a great athlete,” Trump said, before taking a jab at his Democratic rival: “And Brown was not — he was not an athlete. That guy can’t tie his shoes.” For its part Saturday, the Brown team sent a mobile billboard linking Husted’s support for the war in Iran to higher gas prices through Dayton and on the streets near the rally. “Jon Husted has turned his back on working families — he’s only looking out for his billionaire buddies and special interests,” Brown said in a statement from his campaign. Ohio also is home to what polls show is a close race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician who served as the state’s health director under DeWine. Ohioans have not elected a Democrat as governor in 20 years, but at a time when high prices rate as a top-of-mind concern for voters, there are questions about the billionaire Ramaswamy’s appeal, especially in the rural parts of the state. Ramaswamy, like Husted, addressed the crowd early during the rally, and Trump invited both to return to the stage during his speech for additional remarks. Trump introduced Ramaswamy by noting how he had briefly run against him for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination. “He was a nasty guy,” Trump said of Ramaswamy. “But you know what? He was smart. He loves the state. He’s actually got a great heart.” Compared with Husted, Ramaswamy was otherwise less of a focus of Trump’s remarks. Trump, for example, criticized Senate Democrats who this week blocked Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to rein in higher utility costs associated with power-hungry data centers. Republicans, Trump said, are “taking historic action to ensure that Big Tech data centers benefit local communities.” Trump then made the argument for data centers, despite the fears it could be a losing issue for Husted. “We want them,” Trump said. “Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China.” Trump also recited the lyrics to the 1968 Al Wilson song “The Snake” — a recurring, crowd-pleasing bit in his rally speeches — with a new, localized twist. Trump dedicated the song, which he uses as an allegory to trusting communities that welcome immigrants, to nearby Springfield, Ohio. The city became a flashpoint in the 2024 presidential election after Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating dogs and pets. At another point, the crowd broke into chants of “four more years” for the term-limited president. “I’d love to do the four-more-year thing,” Trump responded in a teasing tone before suggesting that the press would overplay his remarks. “We’re driving them totally crazy,” Trump said, referring to the media. “But I love doing it. I love being with you. I really do.”

articles.title: Trump backs data centers in Ohio amid tight Senate race
articles.summary: President Trump defended data centers at a midterm campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio Saturday, arguing that the U.S. will risk losing ground in the global artificial intelligence race against China without the massive facilities that have come under heightened scrutiny in recent years. “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just…
articles.body:
President Trump defended data centers at a midterm campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio Saturday, arguing that the U.S. will risk losing ground in the global artificial intelligence race against China without the massive facilities that have come under heightened scrutiny in recent years.

“There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” Trump told the crowd at a rally in the Buckeye State, where data centers have emerged as a flashpoint in one of the country’s most competitive Senate races.

The president argued that the facilities, which provide the computing power needed to develop and run AI systems —which he has now dubbed “superintelligence” — would be a beneficial investment in Ohio.

He also promised that his administration is working to ensure data centers “benefit local communities.”

Opposition to new data centers has grown across the country, with residents and lawmakers raising concerns about their enormous electricity demands and water usage that could drive up utility bills for consumers.

Backlash over data centers has emerged as a pain point for Republicans ahead of the rapidly approaching midterm elections.

Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President Vance and is currently facing a competitive challenge from former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), has faced criticism over his support for bringing data centers to the state while serving as lieutenant governor.

Husted, who was at the Saturday rally, has introduced a bill that sought to address those concerns by requiring large power users to shoulder more of their costs. The GOP-controlled Senate tried to advance the legislation, but it was ultimately blocked by Senate Democrats.

Brown has sought to make the issue a liability for the Ohio Republican.

“Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio,” Brown wrote Friday on the social platform X . “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

Trump, however, has repeatedly backed the buildout of data centers while dismissing concerns about the rapidly growing and powerful technology as his administration pushes to expand AI infrastructure in the U.S. to compete with China.

articles.title: Aliança Catalana de Sílvia Orriols empataría a escaños con el PSC en Cataluña
articles.standfirst: Según la reciente encuesta de Ipsos para La Vanguardia
articles.summary: Según la reciente encuesta de Ipsos para La Vanguardia
articles.body: Aliança Catalana, de Sílvia Orriols, experimentaría un crecimiento meteórico en las próximas elecciones autonómicas de Cataluña, pasando de los dos escaños a los 30. Así lo plantea la última encuesta de Ipsos para La Vanguardia, realizada entre el 23 de septiembre y el 1 de octubre a 2.000 personas. Según estos resultados, la formación nacionalista empataría con el PSC, de Salvador Illa, formación que actualmente gobierna la Generalitat, que perdería 12 diputados (de 42 a 30). Esquerra Republicana de Cataluña (ERC) pasaría de los 20 escaños a los 23 y, en cuarto puesto, estaría VOX, con una subida notable: pasaría de 11 diputados a 18. El quinto partido político en Cataluña sería Junts, con un descenso enorme en sus resultados: de los 35 actuales, sumaría 16 en los siguientes comicios autonómicos. El Partido Popular (PP) también baja: de 15 bajaría a 11. La mayoría absoluta en Cataluña está cifrada en 68 escaños. Esto plantea un escenario muy complejo en la comunidad autónoma. En base a los resultados de la encuesta de Ipsos, ninguno de los partidos podría alcanzar esta cifra. A no ser que lo hiciera con pactos que, a día de hoy, parecen muy poco probables. La alianza entre PSC (30) y ERC (23), por ejemplo, sumaría 53 escaños. Necesitaría a Junts, lo que se antojaría como una sociedad bastante sorprendente actualmente. Sí existe, numéricamente, la opción de que Aliança Catalana (30), VOX (18), Junts (16) y PP (11) sumen para formar gobierno en la Generalitat. Aunque, de nuevo, se trata de una combinación, sobre el papel, difícil viendo las distintas posturas que defienden las formaciones en cuestiones como el nacionalismo catalán. En definitiva, la encuesta de Ipsos dibuja un escenario de delicada, y virtualmente imposible, gobernabilidad en la comunidad autónoma. Las elecciones en Cataluña podrían celebrarse el próximo 2028.

articles.title: Gonzalo Bernardos, tajante con Pedro Sánchez: "Ha hecho lo que más le conviene para continuar en Moncloa"
articles.standfirst: El economista pone en duda los últimos movimientos del Ejecutivo en materia de vivienda
articles.summary: El economista pone en duda los últimos movimientos del Ejecutivo en materia de vivienda
articles.body: El debate económico, político y social en España vuelve a situar el acceso a la vivienda en el centro de la polémica nacional. El conocido economista y profesor titular de la Universidad de Barcelona, Gonzalo Bernardos, ha arremetido con dureza a través de sus redes sociales contra las recientes medidas regulatorias en materia de alquiler impulsadas por el Gobierno de España, señalando de forma explícita la estrategia política trazada por el presidente del Ejecutivo, Pedro Sánchez. A través de una serie de publicaciones compartidas en su cuenta oficial de la red social X (anteriormente Twitter), Bernardos ha vertido severas críticas sobre las consecuencias negativas que, a su juicio, ocasiona la intervención directa de los precios de los inmuebles. El analista subraya de forma insistente la sólida formación académica del líder socialista para dar mayor solidez a sus argumentos: "Pedro Sánchez es economista y sabe los perjuicios que genera el control de alquileres", sostiene con rotundidad el docente catalán en uno de sus mensajes más comentados. Asimismo, el mediático profesor ha recordado diversas intervenciones públicas donde se contrapone la postura intervencionista actual de la administración con posicionamientos pasados del propio presidente respecto al mercado inmobiliario y la necesidad de mantener la seguridad jurídica. Para el experto, la adopción de topes a las rentas y decretos no responde a criterios técnicos ni a la efectividad real para facilitar el acceso a un hogar, sino a meros cálculos tácticos para la gobernabilidad. "¿Ha hecho lo contrario de lo que piensa? Probablemente, sí. No obstante, ha hecho lo que más le conviene para continuar en Moncloa", sentencia con firmeza el analista. El contundente pronunciamiento del economista no ha tardado en hacerse viral en las plataformas digitales, avivando de forma inmediata la discusión entre defensores de la regulación estatal y aquellos profesionales del sector inmobiliario que advierten sobre el inminente riesgo de contracción en la oferta de pisos y la creciente desconfianza generada entre los pequeños propietarios.
